description: Equipo de la Agrupación Estudiantil UFROMAKERS
summary: AYLEN is a web application that turns two decades of NASA satellite hotspot detections into an integrated burning activity calendar for La Araucanía, Chile. MODIS and VIIRS hotspots cannot be compared point by point, so AYLEN counts "day-cells": a 2 km grid cell with at least one hotspot on a given local day counts once, regardless of how many hotspots or sensors detected it. This avoids counting the same cell-day twice when both sensors observe it and combines their records into one indicator. Users can explore hotspots on an interactive map, compare months with their historical median within each sensor period, identify critical seasonal periods, find places where hotspots recur year after year, and explore 378 historical records with source references, replaying those with known dates. AYLEN is designed to help emergency responders, land managers and researchers understand when and where observed hotspot activity is unusual and anticipate the months that need the most attention
details:
The problem and our response

A change in satellite sensor should not be mistaken for a change in burning activity. MODIS and VIIRS observe different pixel sizes, detection sensitivities and overpass opportunities. Simply joining their hotspot counts can create misleading historical comparisons.

AYLEN addresses the Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots challenge through a working regional prototype: a bilingual geospatial laboratory that connects NASA detections, a burning activity calendar, seasonal analysis and transparent evaluation. Developed by five UFRO Makers students with a professor, it is designed for researchers, municipal planners and land managers who need interpretable historical evidence.

How it works

Traceable observations. The delivered dataset contains 175,486 regional detections prepared from 48 source CSV files, with 302 monthly data files covering 2000–2025. The inventory preserves source filenames, version labels and checksums. Presence of a monthly file does not establish complete observation coverage.

A common spatial and temporal unit. Detections are assigned to grid cells in a Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection centered at 38° S, 72° W. The Advanced view uses a fixed 2 km grid and local dates in America/Santiago. One cell detected on one local day contributes one day-cell. During sensor overlap, the integrated count is MODIS day-cells plus VIIRS day-cells minus their same-cell, same-day intersection. This prevents repeated counting of that unit; it does not identify individual fires or equalize sensor sensitivity.

Historical comparisons with explicit sensor boundaries. The Advanced view separates 2001–2011, using MODIS, from 2012–2025, using MODIS and VIIRS Suomi-NPP. Its baselines start in 2003 and February 2012, respectively. NOAA-20 is available on the map but excluded from this view's baseline to avoid an additional platform change in 2018. Advanced filters retain type 0 or unclassified observations, MODIS confidence at least 30, and nominal/high VIIRS confidence. Anomalies are interpreted within each period, not as a calibrated trend across the sensor transition.

Evaluation instead of assuming a universal cell size. An internal technical view supports configurable cell sizes, seeded Monte Carlo grid shifts and withheld-season reconstruction tests. It reports border sensitivity, reconstruction error and recovery of highly active months. Two kilometers is the demonstration scale, not a universally validated optimum. This evaluation is separate from the fixed-grid Advanced calendar.

What users can do

Explore detections, integrated cells and commune boundaries; inspect satellite, coordinates, date and available attributes.

Compare monthly activity with its historical median, examine seasonal profiles and identify recurrent spatial patterns.

Replay dated historical records, inspect their source and reported area, and compare them with satellite context without automatically attributing detections to an incident.

Filter and export observations, cells and historical tables for further analysis.

The replacement historical CSV contains 378 records: 371 cite CONAF's magnitude-fire publication and seven cite supplementary sources. Preliminary figures remain labelled. Missing coordinates and dates remain missing; AYLEN does not invent fire points or perimeters. This catalogue is contextual information, not completed independent validation of the model.

A reproducible demonstration

With the Advanced view's fixed settings, February 2023 produces 1,815 day-cells against a February reference median of 261, approximately 6.95 times the baseline. January–April contributes 77.2% of the sum of the twelve monthly medians in the 2012–2025 seasonal profile. These are observed-activity indicators, not burned hectares, confirmed incident counts or forecasts.

Value, limits and next steps

AYLEN makes the relationship between observations, aggregation and interpretation inspectable. The browser application requires no account or installation; online basemaps require internet. Its intended contribution is to support seasonal preparedness and further investigation, not issue operational alerts.

Common counting rules do not eliminate differences in detection probability, clouds or observation opportunities. Full cross-era equivalence remains to be established. Next steps are observation-coverage modelling, independent incident-level validation, user testing and predictive models incorporating weather, vegetation and other environmental variables. Predictive prevention is a research goal, not a capability claimed for this release.

The implementation uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Web Workers, Leaflet and Apache ECharts, with Python for preparation and verification. Source code and the standalone HTML are included in the delivery package.
